newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica Mossgas hopes for 1 bln rand gas extension.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica Mossgas hopes for 1 bln rand gas extension.

text.p: State-owned oil from gas producer Mossgas hoped to get government approval later this year to invest about one billion rand in extending the life of its gas reserves, chief executive Dave Day said on Wednesday.
This comes only a year after it received the much contested go-ahead to invest 910 million rand extending the life of its FA gas field off Mossel Bay on the east coast to the year 2000.

Day, who contests the popular view that Mossgas is an apartheid-era white elephant that should be shut down rather than allowed more state funding to keep it alive, said the further extension had to be in place by September 2000.
"It's a 36 month project, so we need to get cracking right away," Day told Reuters after he had briefed the parliamentary minerals and energy committee on Mossgas.
He hoped that the necessary cabinet approval would be obtained without the delays and public wrangling that marked efforts to get approval for the last expansion.

Although Mossgas, part of the state Central Energy Fund (CEF) stable, has been able to report operating profits for the last four years, a large slice of this has been due to state subsidies and pressure has been growing for this to end.
Audited figures show that in 1996/97 Mossgas had an operating profit of 715 million rand compared to 352 million rand in the previous year.
This was made up of a surplus of 626 million rand (40 million rand), tariff protection of 40 million rand (191 million rand) and a synthetc fuel levy of 50 million rand (121 million rand).

Day contests the fact that the last two are classed as subsidies and told the committee that the funds needed to extend the life of Mossgas' gas fields would not come from state coffers but from the CEF's cash flow.

The CEF, however, still owes the state about 10.6 billion rand of the 11.4 billion rand invested in Mossgas so far and one committee member said he could not accept Day's arguement that the taxpayer would not foot the bill.
Day told Reuters that the second of the two new satellite gas fields had been flared and would be coupled to the FA gas platform 85km off Mossel Bay in about a week's time.
Two other satellite fields would go on stream in July and August, but these would only last until the end of 2000, by which time further extensions would be needed.
Mossgas was originally allocated gas fields estimated to have a life of 25 years but it was soon discovered that they would last only 13 years.
Day said it was uncertain how much gas was really available in the Bredasdorp Basin in which the gas fields lie, but there were interesting possibilities that could be explored.
"The most interesting one is the ECN field, which could have as much as 15 years," he said.

Day said that given these possible reserves, Mossgas should be granted a fairer operating regime. He urged that tariff protection should be restored to its $23 a barrel level compared to the present $18.50, which would drop to $17.50 in July in line with the phasing out of tariff protection announced in 1993.
This would enable Mossgass to continue its exploration work and become as profitable as former state-owned oil from coal producer Sasol Ltd SAOJ.J, he said.
"And if the state wanted to privatise Mossgas and float it on the stock exchange, it could do so," Day said.
He said he also wanted Mossgas to get a fairer price for its fuel from the oil industry and develop its export markets.
